parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what two properties of a moving object determine how hard it is to stop - one to do with how much matter it has and one to do with how fast it moves.
parts.proper_answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Momentum Means**
Think of momentum as the quantity of motion an object has. A heavy lorry moving slowly and a light bullet moving very fast can both be hard to stop because both mass and velocity matter.

Step 2: **Exact Definition**
Momentum is defined as $$p = mv$$ where $m$ is mass and $v$ is velocity. It is a vector, so it has direction as well as magnitude, with unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ or $\text{N s}$.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of ball $X$ before the collision.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.1 for ball X - what is its mass and what is its speed just before the collision?
Hint 2: Recall how energy stored due to motion depends on mass linearly but on speed squared - write down the standard relation for kinetic energy.
Hint 3: Substitute $m = 0.24\text{ kg}$ and $v = 2.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and check your units give joules, $\text{J}$, to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick Out the Right Ball**
You need ball X before the collision. From Fig. 2.1, $m_X = 0.24\text{ kg}$ and $v = 2.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Both balls have the same speed but different masses, so be careful to use 0.24 kg.

Step 2: **Use the Kinetic Energy Law**
Energy due to motion is: $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ The $v^2$ means doubling speed gives four times the energy. This is a common slip, so square the speed first.

Step 3: **Calculate**
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.24 \times (2.3)^2$$ $$E_k = 0.12 \times 5.29 = 0.635\text{ J}$$ To 2 significant figures, $E_k = 0.63\text{ J}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The area enclosed by the lines and the time axis in Fig. 2.2 represents the change in momentum of ball $Y$ during the collision.

Determine the magnitude of the change in momentum of ball $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the shape enclosed in Fig. 2.2 between $t = 0$ and $t = 5.0\text{ ms}$ - what simple geometric shape is it and what are its base and height from the axes?
Hint 2: Remember to convert the base from $\text{ms}$ to $\text{s}$ before multiplying, so your impulse comes out in $\text{N s}$.
parts.proper_answer: Change in momentum = area = $\frac{1}{2} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 240 = 0.60\text{ N s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Impulse Is Area**
A force acting for a time causes a change in momentum. Mathematically $F\Delta t = \Delta p$, so the area under an $F$-$t$ graph equals impulse, which equals change in momentum.

Step 2: **Read Base and Height**
Fig. 2.2 is a triangle. Base $= 5.0\text{ ms} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$. Peak height $= 240\text{ N}$ at $t = 3.0\text{ ms}$. Area of triangle is: $$\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$$

Step 3: **Calculate**
$$\Delta p = \frac{1}{2} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 240$$ $$\Delta p = 0.60\text{ N s}$$ This is the magnitude of the change in momentum of Y.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of ball $Y$ after the collision.

markscheme_points.text: (change in velocity of Y) $= 0.60 / 0.12$ $(= 5.0 \text{ m s}^{-1})$; final velocity of Y $= 5.0 - 2.3$ $= 2.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$
or (final momentum of Y) $= 0.60 - 0.12 \times 2.3$ $(= 0.324 \text{ N s})$; final velocity of Y $= 0.324 / 0.12$ $= 2.7 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

hints: Hint 1: Think about directions - ball Y was moving to the left at $2.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the force from X pushes it to the right, so the $0.60\text{ N s}$ impulse acts to reduce its leftward momentum.
Hint 2: Link the change in momentum to the change in speed using $\Delta p = m\Delta v$ with $m = 0.12\text{ kg}$, then subtract from the initial speed to get the final speed.
parts.proper_answer: Change in velocity $= 0.60/0.12 = 5.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$; magnitude of final velocity $= 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to the right.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Change in Velocity**
Impulse changes velocity by: $$\Delta p = m\Delta v$$ So: $$\Delta v = \frac{\Delta p}{m} = \frac{0.60}{0.12} = 5.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is how much velocity is added in the opposite direction to Y's initial motion.

Step 2: **Find Final Speed**
Take left as negative and right as positive, or simply think in magnitudes. Y came in at $2.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ left, and gains $5.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to the right. Net result is to the right with magnitude: $$v = 5.0 - 2.3 = 2.7\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ So Y rebounds.

parts.label: (c)

markscheme_points.text: sloping straight line from (0, 0) to $t = 3.0 \text{ ms}$ and another straight line continuous w
lines showing maximum force of magnitude 240 N
lines wholly in the negative $F$ region of the graph

hints: Hint 1: Think about Newton's third law for the pair X and Y during contact - how do the two forces compare in size and direction at every instant?
Hint 2: Compare the time interval of contact - does X push on Y for a different time than Y pushes on X?
Hint 3: Check the sign convention in Fig. 2.2 and Fig. 2.3 - if $F_Y$ is positive (to the right), which side of the time axis must $F_X$ (to the left) be on, and what peak value should it reach?
parts.proper_answer: Inverted triangle of same shape and timing: straight line from (0,0) to -240 N at 3.0 ms then back to zero at 5.0 ms, wholly below (negative) time axis.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Newton's Third Law**
When X pushes Y to the right with $F_Y$, Y pushes X to the left with $F_X$. At every instant: $$F_X = -F_Y$$ Equal magnitude, opposite direction, acting for the same time.

Step 2: **Mirror the Shape**
So the $F_X$-$t$ graph has exactly the same timing: starts at 0 at $t = 0$, rises linearly to a peak at $t = 3.0\text{ ms}$, falls linearly to zero at $t = 5.0\text{ ms}$.

Step 3: **Fix Magnitude and Sign**
Peak magnitude is still $240\text{ N}$, but because it acts to the left it is negative. Draw the whole triangle below the $t$-axis, from 0 down to $-240\text{ N}$ and back to 0. The area magnitude is still $0.60\text{ N s}$, as expected.
